readings.title: Lazy Jack, part 1: the penny, the milk and the cheese
readings.challenge: Hear a pattern repeat, and notice how each piece of advice comes one day too late.
readings.focus: Jack obeys his mother’s advice exactly, but always for the wrong thing.
readings.context: Flora Annie Steel retold these old English tales. A common is open land shared by a village; spinning is making thread; to bask is to lie lazily in the sun. To hire yourself is to work for someone for a day’s pay. A cowkeeper keeps cows; a lout is a clumsy fellow. The story is read over two nights; let the child say Jack’s answer with you.

excerpt.locator: “Lazy Jack,” from the beginning to the spoilt cream cheese; opens “Once upon a time there was a boy whose name was Jack, and he lived with his mother on a…”; closes “"I'll do so another time," replied Jack.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jack’s mother tell him he must go to work?
facilitatorNotes: He is so lazy that he does nothing but lie in the sun or sit by the fire, and she will turn him out if he does not earn his porridge.
evidence: So they called him Lazy Jack.
if he did not begin to work for his porridge

questions.prompt: What is Jack paid each day, and what goes wrong with it?
facilitatorNotes: A penny, which he loses crossing a brook; a jar of milk, which spills from his pocket; and a cream cheese, which spoils on his head.
evidence: he lost it in passing over a brook.
spilling it all, long before he got home.

questions.prompt: Jack always says, “I’ll do so another time.” Does he do what his mother says? What is the joke?
facilitatorNotes: He does exactly what she said, but with the next thing, which needs carrying a different way. Ask the child to guess how he will carry tomorrow’s pay, now that she has said “in your hands.”
evidence: you should have carried it very carefully in your hands.
"I'll do so another time," replied Jack.

readings.title: Lazy Jack, part 2: the cat, the mutton and the donkey
readings.challenge: Follow the pattern to a surprise that turns Jack’s silliness into luck.
readings.focus: Carrying a donkey on his shoulders, Jack makes a girl laugh who had never laughed, and his foolishness makes his fortune.
readings.context: Recap: Lazy Jack’s mother sent him out to work. Each day he carried his pay the way she said he should have carried the thing before, so the penny, the milk and the cheese were all lost or spoilt. A tom-cat is a male cat; mutton is sheep’s meat, and a shoulder of mutton is a big piece of it; a ninney-hammer is a silly person; heehawing is a donkey’s bray.
readings.contentNote: A rich man’s daughter who cannot hear or speak is described with the old phrase “deaf and dumb,” and her father promises her in marriage to whoever makes her laugh.

excerpt.locator: “Lazy Jack,” from the baker’s tom-cat to the end of the tale; opens “Now the next day, Lazy Jack again went out, and hired himself to a baker, who would give…”; closes “…in a large house, and Jack's mother lived with them in great happiness until she died.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jack carry the tom-cat, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: Very carefully in his hands, as his mother had said for the cheese; the cat scratches him so much that he lets it go.
evidence: began carrying it very carefully in his hands,
pussy scratched him so much that he was compelled to let it go.

questions.prompt: Why is his mother out of patience after the mutton?
facilitatorNotes: He dragged it on a string through the dirt and spoilt it, and with no meat for Sunday she had only cabbage for dinner.
evidence: trailed it along after him in the dirt,
she was obliged to do with cabbage for her dinner.

questions.prompt: Why does the rich man’s daughter laugh? How does Jack’s silliness turn out well?
facilitatorNotes: The sight of Jack with a kicking, braying donkey on his shoulders is so funny that she laughs, and she can hear and speak again. Jack marries her and becomes rich, and his mother lives with them. Children may say Jack was lucky rather than clever; the tale enjoys that.
evidence: the poor beast with its legs sticking up in the air
she burst out into a great fit of laughter,

readings.title: The Three Sillies, part 1: the mallet in the cellar
readings.challenge: Follow a long chain of “supposing” and decide whether the danger is real.
readings.focus: A girl imagines a whole future just to worry about it, and her mother sits down and cries with her.
readings.context: This English folk tale is read over five nights. A squire is a young gentleman who owns land, and the Hall is his big house; to court someone is to visit them hoping to marry. A cellar is a cool room under the house; cider is an apple drink kept in a barrel, or cask, with a tap. A mallet is a heavy wooden hammer; a beam holds up the ceiling. “Lawks a mercy me!” means “Goodness me!” Read each “supposing” a little faster than the one before.
readings.contentNote: The daughter imagines a future son killed by the falling mallet; nothing happens to anyone.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Sillies,” from the beginning to the daughter and her mother crying together; opens “Once upon a time, when folk were not so wise as they are nowadays, there lived a farmer…”; closes “So they both sat a-crying.”.

questions.prompt: What does the daughter see when she looks up at the cellar ceiling?
facilitatorNotes: A big wooden mallet stuck in a beam, all covered in cobwebs, which she had never noticed before.
evidence: there she saw a big wooden mallet stuck in one of the beams.
It must have been there for ages and ages,

questions.prompt: What does she imagine could happen? Count the “supposings” on your fingers.
facilitatorNotes: That she marries the squire, they have a son, he grows up, comes down to draw cider, and the mallet falls on him. Every step is only “supposing”; none of it has happened.
evidence: supposing the mallet were to fall on his head and kill him

questions.prompt: Has anything bad happened yet? What is really going wrong in the cellar while they cry?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing has happened, and the mallet has hung there for ages. Meanwhile the cider tap is still open and the cider is running all over the floor: a real mess made by worrying about a pretend one.
evidence: the cider running all over the floor.

readings.title: The Three Sillies, part 2: the squire’s promise
readings.challenge: Notice who joins the crying and who stops it.
readings.focus: The father cries too; the squire turns off the tap, pulls out the mallet, and sets himself a test before he will marry.
readings.context: Recap: the farmer’s daughter saw an old mallet in the cellar ceiling and cried at the thought that it might one day fall on a son she does not even have; her mother sat down and cried with her while the cider ran over the floor. “Zounds!” is an old cry of surprise; man’s estate means grown up. Sillies are foolish people.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Sillies,” from the farmer going down to the cellar to the squire setting off on his travels; opens “Now after a time, when they did not come back, the farmer began to wonder what had…”; closes “…again on his travels, leaving them all crying; this time because the marriage was off!”.

questions.prompt: Who comes down to the cellar next, and what does he do?
facilitatorNotes: The farmer, the girl’s father. When he hears about the mallet, he sits down and cries too.
evidence: started a-crying too.

questions.prompt: What two things does the squire do that nobody else thought of?
facilitatorNotes: He turns off the tap, and he pulls the mallet out and puts it safely on the floor. Both take a moment; the danger is gone.
evidence: the first thing he did was to run straight and turn off the tap.
he reached up to the old mallet and pulled it out, and put it safe on the floor.

questions.prompt: What does the squire decide to do before he will marry the daughter? Is that a fair test?
facilitatorNotes: He will travel, and come back to marry her only if he finds three people sillier than her family. Some children will think it is unkind, since they are left crying; others will find it fair or funny. Ask what they think he will find.
evidence: if I can find three bigger sillies than you three, then I'm come back and be married--not otherwise.
this time because the marriage was off!

readings.title: The Three Sillies, part 3: the cow on the roof
readings.challenge: Compare the squire’s easy idea with the old woman’s plan, and predict what will go wrong.
readings.focus: An old woman refuses good advice, and her clever-sounding plan ends in disaster.
readings.context: Recap: the squire found the farmer’s family crying over trouble that might never happen. He pulled out the mallet and set off to find three bigger sillies before he would marry the daughter. A thatched roof is made of straw, and grass can grow on it. To cudgel is to beat with a stick; durst not means dared not; flustered means hot and muddled; obstinate means stubborn; coaxed and codgered mean begged and wheedled; a hullabaloo is a great noise.
readings.contentNote: The old woman beats her cow to make it climb. The cow falls off the roof and is strangled by the rope, and the old woman is pulled up the chimney and smothered in soot; it is told in one sentence, as a joke.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Sillies,” from the old woman’s cottage to the squire finding the first bigger silly; opens “Well, the young man travelled far and he travelled fast, but never did he find a bigger…”; closes “…is one bigger silly," quoth the young squire as he journeyed on. "So now for two more!"”.

questions.prompt: What is the old woman trying to make her cow do?
facilitatorNotes: Climb a ladder onto the roof to eat the grass growing there. The cow is afraid and will not go.
evidence: cudgel her cow into going up a ladder to eat the grass.

questions.prompt: What easier way does the squire suggest, and what does the old woman answer?
facilitatorNotes: She could climb up herself, cut the grass, and throw it down. She says a cow can cut grass for herself and tells him to mind his own business.
evidence: It would be easier if you went up the ladder, cut the grass, and threw it down for the cow to eat.
So mind your own business, young sir.

questions.prompt: Why does the squire call her “one bigger silly” than the farmer’s family?
facilitatorNotes: The family cried over a danger that was not real; she would not listen to good advice, and her plan for a real danger went badly wrong. Children may also say she was silly to think a rope would keep the cow safe.
evidence: That is one bigger silly,
she can't fall off the roof without my knowing it.

readings.title: The Three Sillies, part 4: the breeches
readings.challenge: Picture a silly way of doing an everyday job, and the sensible way.
readings.focus: A pleasant stranger has spent years jumping into his trousers each morning, and is grateful to be shown how.
readings.context: Recap: the squire is travelling to find three people sillier than the farmer’s family before he will marry their daughter. He has found one: an old woman who would not listen to his advice about her cow. An inn is a place where travellers sleep; breeches are trousers that end at the knee; a tallboy is a tall chest of drawers with knobs. Foregathered means made friends. Act out the stranger’s run and jump.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Sillies,” from the crowded inn to the stranger learning to put on his breeches; opens “He did not find any, however, till late one night he arrived at a little inn. And the inn…”; closes “…and the stranger was ever so grateful and said he never should have thought of that way.”.

questions.prompt: How does the stranger try to put on his breeches?
facilitatorNotes: He hangs them on the knobs of the tallboy, runs from the other end of the room, and tries to jump into them, again and again.
evidence: takes a little run, and tried to jump into the breeches.

questions.prompt: How long does this take him every morning?
facilitatorNotes: The best part of an hour, and it makes him hot and sweaty.
evidence: It takes me the best part of an hour every morning before I get them on.

questions.prompt: The squire laughs, but he also helps. Is the stranger a different kind of silly from the old woman with the cow?
facilitatorNotes: Yes: he asks “How do you manage yours?” and is grateful to learn, while she refused help. Children may say he is still a bigger silly for never having thought of it; both are fair.
evidence: How do you manage yours?
the stranger was ever so grateful and said he never should have thought of that way.

readings.title: The Three Sillies, part 5: the moon in the pond
readings.challenge: Tell something real from its reflection, and hear how the story ends.
readings.focus: A whole village tries to rake the moon out of a pond, and the squire decides there are sillies everywhere.
readings.context: Recap: the squire has found two people sillier than the farmer’s family, an old woman with a cow on her roof and a man who jumped into his trousers; he needs one more before he will go back and marry the farmer’s daughter. Rakes, pitchforks and brooms are long-handled tools. “Can't ee see” is country speech for “Can’t you see”; nohow means in any way. To abuse someone roundly is to shout insults at them; to duck someone is to push them under water. If you can, show the child a reflection in a spoon or a puddle first.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Sillies,” from the village pond to the end of the tale; opens “"So that," quoth young squire to himself, "is a second bigger silly." But he travelled…”; closes “…didn't live happy ever after, that has nothing to do with the story of the three sillies.”.

questions.prompt: What are the villagers doing at the pond, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Raking, forking and sweeping the water, because they think the moon has fallen in and they cannot get her out.
evidence: Can't ee see moon's fallen into the pond, an' we can't get her out nohow?

questions.prompt: Where is the moon really? Why won’t the villagers believe the squire?
facilitatorNotes: Up in the sky, shining broad and full; the moon in the pond is only a reflection. They will not look up, and they get angry with him instead.
evidence: bade them look up over their heads where the moon was riding broad and full.
they wouldn't believe that what they saw in the water was only a reflection.

questions.prompt: Why does the squire go back and marry the farmer’s daughter after all? Do you like his reason?
facilitatorNotes: He has found that there are sillies everywhere, so she is “no sillier than the rest.” Some children will find that a kind ending; others will say it is not a very loving reason, which the last line jokes about too.
evidence: There are many more sillies in this world than I thought for;
She is no sillier than the rest.

readings.title: Titty Mouse and Tatty Mouse, part 1: the stool, the broom and the walnut tree
readings.challenge: Keep a growing list in order: each new thing repeats everything that happened before it.
readings.focus: One sad event sets off a silly chain of things that copy one another.
readings.context: Flora Annie Steel retold these old English tales. To glean is to gather the grain left in a field after harvest, and an ear of corn is the grainy top of a stalk. A form is a long wooden bench; to jar is to bang and rattle. This nonsense chain story is read over two nights; let the child chant the growing list with you.
readings.contentNote: Titty Mouse is scalded to death when the pot tips over, and Tatty weeps; the household things answer with silly actions.

excerpt.locator: “Titty Mouse and Tatty Mouse,” from the beginning to the walnut tree shedding its leaves; opens “Titty Mouse and Tatty Mouse both lived in a house.”; closes “…tree, "I'll shed my leaves." So the walnut tree shed all its beautiful green leaves.”.

questions.prompt: What do Titty Mouse and Tatty Mouse both do at the start?
facilitatorNotes: Everything together: they both glean, both find an ear of corn and both make a pudding. The doubled sentences set up the pattern.
evidence: So they both went a-gleaning.
So they both made a pudding.

questions.prompt: What happens when Titty puts her pudding into the pot?
facilitatorNotes: The pot tumbles over and scalds her to death, and Tatty sits down and weeps. This is the event that starts the whole chain.
evidence: the pot tumbled over, and scalded her to death, and Tatty sat down and wept.

questions.prompt: The stool hops, the broom sweeps and the door jars. Why does each one do something?
facilitatorNotes: Each hears the news from the one before and adds its own action, as if sharing Tatty’s sorrow in its own odd way. Children may find it funny that a stool hops for sadness; the story holds both the joke and the sorrow.
evidence: "Then," said the stool, "I'll hop," so the stool hopped.
So the walnut tree shed all its beautiful green leaves.

readings.title: Titty Mouse and Tatty Mouse, part 2: everything comes tumbling down
readings.challenge: Follow the chain to its biggest link, then hear everything fall at once.
readings.focus: The chain grows until it brings the whole house down in one long tumble.
readings.context: Recap: when Titty Mouse died, Tatty wept, and then the stool, the broom, the door, the window, the old bench and the walnut tree each did something odd. To moult is to lose feathers; a pitcher is a jug; thatching a rick means covering a haystack with straw. Let the child join in on the long list.
readings.contentNote: An old man falls from a ladder and breaks his neck, and the house falls on Tatty Mouse.

excerpt.locator: “Titty Mouse and Tatty Mouse,” from the little bird to the end of the tale; opens “Now there was a little bird perched on one of the boughs of the tree, and when all the…”; closes “…and the broom upset the stool, and poor little Tatty Mouse was buried beneath the ruins.”.

questions.prompt: What does the little bird do, and what does the little girl do?
facilitatorNotes: The bird moults all its feathers, and the girl drops her jug and spills the milk meant for supper.
evidence: so he moulted all his gay feathers.
So she dropt the pitcher and spilt the milk.

questions.prompt: Why is the old man cross with the little girl?
facilitatorNotes: Her brothers and sisters will go without their supper. He is the first to see what a silly action costs, and then he does something sillier still.
evidence: your little brothers and sisters must go without their suppers.

questions.prompt: The last sentence knocks everything down. What falls first, and who is under it all at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The great walnut tree falls first, and then the bench, the house, the window, the door, the broom and the stool, until Tatty Mouse is buried. The fall runs back through the chain; children can name a few in order with help.
evidence: the great walnut tree fell down with a crash
poor little Tatty Mouse was buried beneath the ruins.

readings.title: The Three Little Pigs, part 1: straw and furze
readings.challenge: Hear a pattern happen twice and get ready for a third time.
readings.focus: Two polite pigs are given building things, but houses of straw and furze cannot keep out the wolf.
readings.context: A sow is a mother pig; to seek your fortune is to go out and make your own way. Furze is a prickly bush, also called gorse. “By the hair of my chinny chin chin” is a pig’s promise. Use a big voice for the wolf and a small one for the pigs; the story goes on for four nights.
readings.contentNote: The wolf blows down two houses and eats the first two pigs.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Little Pigs,” from the beginning to the wolf eating the second pig; opens “Once upon a time there was an old sow who had three little pigs, and as she had not…”; closes “…and he puffed and he blew the house in. Then he ate up little piggy and went on his way.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the old sow send her pigs out into the world?
facilitatorNotes: She has not enough food for them, so they must seek their fortunes.
evidence: as she had not enough for them to eat

questions.prompt: Why does the man give the first little pig his straw?
facilitatorNotes: Because the pig asks so politely: the man likes his good manners. The second man gives his furze for the same reason.
evidence: If you please, sir, could you give me that straw to build me a house?
seeing what good manners the little pig had

questions.prompt: What does each pig see through the keyhole? What might the third pig see?
facilitatorNotes: The first sees the wolf’s big paws and the second his great ears, so each knows it is the wolf. Ask what the third pig might see; the story answers next time.
evidence: saw the wolf's big paws through the keyhole
saw the wolf's great ears

readings.title: The Three Little Pigs, part 2: the brick house and the turnips
readings.challenge: Notice where the pattern breaks, and how the pig gets the better of a trick.
readings.focus: The brick house holds, so the wolf turns to tricks, and the pig is cleverer than he is.
readings.context: Recap: an old sow sent her three pigs to seek their fortunes; the wolf blew in the straw house and the furze house and ate the first two pigs. Now the third pig asks for bricks. Chaff is the dry husk of grain, so “not one to be taken in with chaff” means not easily fooled. A sluggard is a lazy slowcoach.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Little Pigs,” from the third pig and the bricks to the turnip breakfast; opens “Now the third little piggy, when he started, met a man carrying a load of bricks, and,…”; closes “…to the field and come back again, and I'm having a nice potful of turnips for breakfast."”.

questions.prompt: What happens when the wolf huffs and puffs at the brick house?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot blow it down and runs out of breath. The pattern of the first two houses breaks here.
evidence: but he could not blow the house down.

questions.prompt: Why does the wolf want the pig to go to the turnip field with him?
facilitatorNotes: So he can catch the pig outside his strong house and eat him; the turnips are only bait.
evidence: I know where there is ever such a nice field of turnips.
if you will be ready at six o'clock to-morrow morning

questions.prompt: How does the little pig trick the wolf?
facilitatorNotes: He gets up at five, fetches the turnips and is home eating them when the wolf arrives, then calls the wolf a sluggard. Ask why the pig did not tell the wolf his plan.
evidence: so he got up at five
Why! what a sluggard you are!

readings.title: The Three Little Pigs, part 3: the apple tree
readings.challenge: Compare the wolf’s second trick with his first and see what he has learned.
readings.focus: This time the wolf sets out early too, so the pig must think fast up in the tree.
readings.context: Recap: the wolf could not blow down the brick house, and the third pig fooled him by fetching the turnips an hour early. Now the wolf tries again with apples. Merry gardens is an orchard; “an early bird” is someone up before everyone else.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Little Pigs,” from the wolf’s second offer to the pig running home with his apples; opens “Then the wolf grew red with rage; but he was determined to eat little piggy, so he said,…”; closes “…gone to pick it up, the little pig was able to jump down with his basket and run home.”.

questions.prompt: What does the wolf offer this time, and at what time?
facilitatorNotes: Apples from a tree in Merry gardens, at five o’clock the next morning.
evidence: A nice apple tree down in Merry gardens
if you will be ready at five o'clock to-morrow morning

questions.prompt: Why does the wolf set out at four o’clock this time?
facilitatorNotes: He was fooled once and will not be fooled again: he has learned the pig’s trick.
evidence: the wolf had been taken in once and wasn't going to be taken in again

questions.prompt: How does the pig escape from the tree?
facilitatorNotes: He throws an apple far away, and while the wolf goes after it he jumps down and runs home. Ask whether this trick is cleverer than the turnip trick.
evidence: I'll throw you down one to try.
And he threw it so far away

readings.title: The Three Little Pigs, part 4: the butter-churn and the chimney
readings.challenge: Follow the last two tricks and decide whether the ending fits the story.
readings.focus: A rolling churn frightens the wolf, and when he tries the chimney the pig is ready for him.
readings.context: Recap: the third pig has fooled the wolf twice, getting the turnips early and escaping from the apple tree by throwing an apple. A fairing is a present bought at a fair; a butter-churn is a wooden barrel for making butter. “As mild as milk” means gently, pretending to be kind.
readings.contentNote: The wolf falls into a pot of boiling water, and the pig cooks and eats him.

excerpt.locator: “The Three Little Pigs,” from the invitation to the fair to the end of the tale; opens “Well, the wolf was fair angry; but he went next day to the little piggy's house and…”; closes “So the little piggy put on the cover again, boiled the wolf up, and ate him for supper.”.

questions.prompt: What does the pig buy at the fair, and how does it save him?
facilitatorNotes: A butter-churn. He hides in it, and it rolls down the hill at the wolf and frightens him away.
evidence: bought himself a butter-churn as a fairing
Bumpety, bumpety, bump!

questions.prompt: What does the wolf think the rolling churn was, and what does the pig tell him?
facilitatorNotes: An awful, dreadful, terrible Thing; the pig cheerfully says it was only him. Ask why telling the truth this time makes the wolf so angry.
evidence: an awful, dreadful, terrible Thing
that must have been me!

questions.prompt: How is the pig ready when the wolf comes down the chimney?
facilitatorNotes: He has a blazing fire and a big pot of water boiling, so the wolf falls in. Some children find the ending fair after all the wolf has done, and some find it too much; both can point to the story.
evidence: the little pig made up a blazing fire and put on a big pot full of water to boil

readings.title: Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar, part 1: the broken pickle-jar
readings.challenge: Meet two characters who meet the same accident in opposite ways.
readings.focus: Mrs. Vinegar breaks their pickle-jar house and cries; cheerful Mr. Vinegar decides they will seek their fortune, carrying the door.
readings.context: This English folk tale is read over five nights. Vinegar is a sour liquid used to pickle vegetables, so a pickle-jar is just the right house for the Vinegars. Snug means cosy; to till a garden is to dig it; clean as a new pin means spotless. Mettle means spirit; to seek your fortune is to go out looking for a way to get rich; quoth means said; trudged means walked heavily.

excerpt.locator: “Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar,” from the beginning to the couple setting out with their door; opens “Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar, a worthy couple, lived in a glass pickle-jar. The house, though…”; closes “…to seek fortune, Mr. Vinegar bearing the door on his back like a snail carries its house.”.

questions.prompt: How does the pickle-jar house get broken?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Vinegar loses her temper with a cobweb and sweeps so hard that the broom handle goes right through the glass.
evidence: she lost her temper with a cobweb
the broom-handle went right through the glass

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Vinegar feel about it, and how does Mr. Vinegar feel? What does he say?
facilitatorNotes: She cries bitterly; he stays cheerful and says, “Accidents will happen, lovey!” and that they can buy another jar if they find money.
evidence: And with that she fell to crying bitterly.
Accidents will happen, lovey!

questions.prompt: Mr. Vinegar takes the door so that nobody can open it. Is that a clever idea? Why does Mrs. Vinegar say nothing?
facilitatorNotes: It is silly, because there is no house left behind the door to keep anyone out of. She cannot see how it helps but keeps quiet. Some children may guess the door will be useful later; the next night shows whether they are right.
evidence: Then no one will be able to open it, will they?
Mrs. Vinegar did not quite see how this fact would mend matters

readings.title: Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar, part 2: the robbers under the tree
readings.challenge: Follow a frightening night that ends in luck nobody planned.
readings.focus: Mr. Vinegar’s trembling shakes the door, with his sleeping wife on it, down onto a band of robbers, who run off and leave their gold.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Vinegar broke the pickle-jar the Vinegars lived in, and cheerful Mr. Vinegar said they would go out and seek their fortune; he carried their door on his back. A brass farthing is a tiny coin; the fork of a tree is where a branch splits; spoils and booty are stolen goods; an aspen is a tree whose leaves tremble in the lightest breeze; to parcel out is to share out. Guineas are gold coins. Whisper the robbers’ part.
readings.contentNote: The door falls on a band of robbers; in the morning one is found “squashed flat as a pancake,” told as a joke.

excerpt.locator: “Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar,” from the night in the forest to the forty golden guineas; opens “Well, they walked all day long, but not a brass farthing did they make, and when night…”; closes “My goodness! How Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar jumped for joy!”.

questions.prompt: Where do the Vinegars sleep in the forest?
facilitatorNotes: Up a tree, on the door, which Mr. Vinegar fixes in a fork of the branches so his wife will be safe from wild beasts.
evidence: fix the door firmly in a fork

questions.prompt: Mr. Vinegar whispers, “It is only the wind in the trees.” Is that true? What is really shaking the door?
facilitatorNotes: No. He is trembling with fear as he listens to the robbers below, though he does not want his wife to know.
evidence: It is only the wind in the trees.
he was not really very brave inside

questions.prompt: How did the Vinegars get their gold: by bravery, by cleverness, or by luck?
facilitatorNotes: Mostly luck: his shaking knocked the door down, and the robbers thought the sky had fallen and ran. Some children may give him credit for the door idea; the tale lets them argue.
evidence: they thought the sky had fallen
forty golden guineas all scattered about!

readings.title: Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar, part 3: the red cow
readings.challenge: Listen for a good plan, and for the moment it starts to go wrong.
readings.focus: Mrs. Vinegar sends her husband to buy a cow, and he pays everything he has for the first one he sees.
readings.context: Recap: the Vinegars lost their pickle-jar house and spent a night in a tree; by luck their door fell on a band of robbers, who ran off and left forty golden guineas. A market-town is a town where people buy and sell animals and goods. “Money makes the mare to go” is an old saying: money gets things done. A bargain is a good buy; a simpleton is someone easily fooled; proud as Punch means very pleased with yourself.

excerpt.locator: “Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar,” from Mrs. Vinegar’s plan to Mr. Vinegar leading off the cow; opens “"Now, Vinegar!" said his wife when they had gathered up all the gold pieces, "I will tell…”; closes “…cow, marching her up and down the market, much against her will, to show off his bargain.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Vinegar want a cow instead of keeping the money?
facilitatorNotes: Money gets spent, but a cow stays and gives milk and butter they can sell, so they will live in comfort.
evidence: Now a cow won't run away, but will give us milk and butter, which we can sell.

questions.prompt: Mr. Vinegar says he always makes good bargains. Which two does he name?
facilitatorNotes: Marrying such a clever wife, and shaking her down from the tree onto the robbers. He ends, “I am the happiest man alive!”
evidence: I made a better one when I shook her down from the tree.
I am the happiest man alive!

questions.prompt: How much does Mr. Vinegar pay for the cow? Was it a good bargain? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: Everything in his pocket, all forty guineas. The owner asks that much because he sees Mr. Vinegar is a simpleton, so it was not a good bargain. Some children may say he got what he wanted; ask what Mrs. Vinegar would say.
evidence: What you've got in your pocket.
seeing he was a simpleton

readings.title: Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar, part 4: bagpipes and gloves
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of swaps and keep track of what Mr. Vinegar has after each one.
readings.focus: Each time Mr. Vinegar sees something new, he swaps what he has for it, sure that it will make him the happiest man alive.
readings.context: Recap: the Vinegars found forty gold guineas, and Mrs. Vinegar sent her husband to market to buy a cow. He paid all forty for an old red cow. Bagpipes are played by blowing into a bag and fingering holes in the pipes; they are hard to play. A livelihood is a way of earning a living; churning is shaking cream until it becomes butter; hootings and peltings are jeers and things thrown.

excerpt.locator: “Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar,” from the bagpiper in the market to Mr. Vinegar setting off home with the gloves; opens “Now, as he drove it about, proud as Punch, he noticed a man who was playing the bagpipes.…”; closes “…pleased with himself. "Warm hands, warm heart!" he thought. "I'm the happiest man alive!"”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Vinegar want the bagpipes?
facilitatorNotes: The piper has children dancing after him and pennies showering into his cap; Mr. Vinegar thinks that is easier than feeding and milking a cow.
evidence: a perfect shower of pennies fell into his cap
That is an easier way of earning a livelihood than by driving about a beast of a cow!

questions.prompt: What happens when Mr. Vinegar tries to play?
facilitatorNotes: At first no sound at all, then a terrible squeal that sends the children running and makes people cover their ears. He earns nothing.
evidence: such a terrific squeal and screech that all the children ran away frightened

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Vinegar say each time he wants something new? Does it come true?
facilitatorNotes: That he would be the happiest man alive if he had it. He is happy for a moment after each swap, but each one leaves him with something worth less. Some children may admire how cheerful he stays.
evidence: I should be the happiest man alive if I had those bagpipes!
I'm the happiest man alive!

readings.title: Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar, part 5: the magpie
readings.challenge: Hear all of Mr. Vinegar’s bargains added up, and decide what he has learned.
readings.focus: A laughing magpie tells Mr. Vinegar the truth, and he goes home with nothing at all.
readings.context: Recap: Mr. Vinegar went to market with forty gold guineas. He paid them all for a cow, swapped the cow for bagpipes he could not play, and the bagpipes for a pair of warm gloves. A stout stick is a strong walking stick; a magpie is a black-and-white bird with a loud, chattering call; forsooth means truly; a blockhead is a foolish person; guffaws are loud laughs. To turn over a new leaf is to start again and do better; a housemaid is paid to clean a house.
readings.contentNote: When Mr. Vinegar comes home with nothing, his wife beats him; it is told in one sentence as part of the joke, and he says she nearly broke every bone in his body.

excerpt.locator: “Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar,” from the man with the stick to the end of the tale; opens “But as he trudged he grew very, very tired, and at last began to limp. Then he saw a man…”; closes “And that is the story of Mr. and Mrs. Vinegar.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Vinegar swap his gloves for, and why?
facilitatorNotes: A stick, because he is tired and limping and thinks warm hands are no use if his feet ache.
evidence: What is the use of warm hands if your feet ache!

questions.prompt: The magpie counts up all his bargains. Tell them in order, from the forty guineas to the stick.
facilitatorNotes: Forty guineas for a cow, the cow for bagpipes, the bagpipes for gloves, the gloves for a stick, and then the stick is lost in a tree. Children can count on their fingers.
evidence: You bought a cow for forty guineas when she wasn't worth ten,
and the pair of gloves for a miserable stick.

questions.prompt: At the end Mr. Vinegar says almost what he said at the very beginning: there are good jars in the shop. Has he changed, or not?
facilitatorNotes: He is still cheerful and ready to start again, so in one way he has not changed. But this time he plans to work as a gardener to earn the money, which may show he has learned something. Children may argue either way.
evidence: I think we had better turn over a new leaf and begin afresh.
There are as good ones in the shop as ever came out of it.

readings.title: Henny-Penny, part 1: the sky is falling
readings.challenge: Remember the friends in order as the line of walkers grows.
readings.focus: A hen mistakes a falling acorn for the falling sky, and every bird she meets believes her.
readings.context: In this old tale each new animal joins the line, and the list of names grows every time. A rickyard is a farmyard where the haystacks stand. Henny-penny is a hen; her friends are a cock, a duck, a goose and a turkey. Say the growing list of names together.

excerpt.locator: “Henny-Penny,” from the beginning to Turkey-lurkey joining the others; opens “One day Henny-penny was picking up corn in the rickyard when--whack!--an acorn hit her…”; closes “…Goosey-poosey, and Turkey-lurkey all went to tell the King the sky was a-falling.”.

questions.prompt: What really hits Henny-penny on the head, and what does she think it means?
facilitatorNotes: An acorn; she thinks the sky is falling and sets off to tell the King.
evidence: an acorn hit her upon the head
the sky's a-going to fall; I must go and tell the King.

questions.prompt: Who joins Henny-penny on the road? Can you say them in order?
facilitatorNotes: Cocky-locky, Ducky-daddles, Goosey-poosey and Turkey-lurkey. Help with the first sounds if needed.
evidence: till she met Cocky-locky
till they met Turkey-lurkey

questions.prompt: Does anyone ask Henny-penny how she knows the sky is falling? Why might that matter?
facilitatorNotes: No one asks; each just asks to come along. If someone had asked, they might have found the acorn. Children may say the birds trusted their friend, which is also true.
evidence: "May I come with you?" says Cocky-locky.
So Henny-penny and Cocky-locky went to tell the King the sky was falling.

readings.title: Henny-Penny, part 2: Foxy-woxy’s short cut
readings.challenge: Spot the trick before the birds do.
readings.focus: A fox offers to show the way, and only Henny-penny escapes, by luck rather than good sense.
readings.context: Recap: an acorn fell on Henny-penny, and she set off to tell the King the sky was falling, with Cocky-locky, Ducky-daddles, Goosey-poosey and Turkey-lurkey behind her. A burrow is an animal’s hole in the ground; a short cut is a quicker way. Read Foxy-woxy’s words smoothly and kindly, as a trickster would speak.
readings.contentNote: Foxy-woxy snaps off the heads of four of the birds; Henny-penny escapes.

excerpt.locator: “Henny-Penny,” from meeting Foxy-woxy to the end of the tale; opens “So they went along, and they went along, and they went along, till they met Foxy-woxy,…”; closes “…bustled off to her nest; so she escaped, but she never told the King the sky was falling!”.

questions.prompt: What does Foxy-woxy offer to do, and where does his “short cut” really lead?
facilitatorNotes: He offers to show the proper way to the King, but the dark hole is the door of his own burrow.
evidence: I know the proper way; shall I show it you?
Now this was the door of Foxy-woxy's burrow.

questions.prompt: Why does Henny-penny turn round and go home?
facilitatorNotes: She hears Cocky-locky crow and thinks it is dawn, time to lay her egg. She escapes by luck, not because she saw the danger.
evidence: My goodness! it must be dawn. Time for me to lay my egg.

questions.prompt: Did Henny-penny ever tell the King? What do you think this story teaches?
facilitatorNotes: No. One lesson: check before believing something big, and be careful of strangers who offer help. Children may find other lessons; ask which bird they would warn, and what they would say.
evidence: she never told the King the sky was falling!

readings.title: The Wee Bannock, part 1: away it trundles
readings.challenge: Meet a busy household and a runaway that starts a chase.
readings.focus: When the old man bites one oatcake, the other jumps up and rolls away.
readings.context: This Scottish tale is read over five nights. Wee means little, and a bannock is a flat round oatcake toasted by the fire. A burnie is a little stream. A spindle and a distaff are tools for spinning wool into thread. “Sho! Sho!” is how you shoo cats away. To trundle is to roll along.

excerpt.locator: “The Wee Bannock,” from the beginning to the old wife giving up the chase; opens “Once upon a time there was an old man and his old wife who lived in a wee cottage beside…”; closes “…out of sight, and the old wife was obliged to go back and tussle with the kittens again.”.

questions.prompt: Who looks after what in the old couple’s cottage?
facilitatorNotes: The old man looks after the cows, the cock the hens, the cat a mouse, and the kittens “look after” the old wife’s spindle, which really means they play with it. Children may enjoy the joke.
evidence: the cock looked after the hens,
the two kittens looked after the old wife's spindle

questions.prompt: Why does the second bannock run away?
facilitatorNotes: The old man took a bite out of the first one, so the other decided it was time to be off.
evidence: takes up one of them and snaps a piece out of it.
the other bannock thought it high time to be off,

questions.prompt: Can the old wife catch it? What do you think will happen to the bannock next?
facilitatorNotes: No: it rolls faster than she can run, so she goes back to the kittens. Let children guess where it goes; the next night tells.
evidence: But the wee bannock trundled faster than she could run,

readings.title: The Wee Bannock, part 2: the tailors and the weaver
readings.challenge: Follow a chase through two houses and notice how the bannock escapes each time.
readings.focus: Grown people with scissors, irons and boards cannot catch one little oatcake.
readings.context: Recap: an old woman baked two wee oatcakes; when her husband bit one, the other jumped up and rolled away. Tailors make clothes, and apprentices are learners; a goose here is a tailor’s heavy iron; carders are combs for wool. A weaver makes cloth on a loom; a clue of yarn is a ball of thread. “Hout-tout!” means “Nonsense!”; “a-feared” is afraid; “yon’s” is “that is”; “the morn” is this morning.
readings.contentNote: An apprentice falls into the hot ashes and is badly burnt.

excerpt.locator: “The Wee Bannock,” from the tailors’ house to the weaver’s door; opens “The wee bannock meanwhile trundled gaily down the hill till it came to a big thatched…”; closes “…was out at the door, trundling away over the hill like a new tarred sheep or a mad cow!”.

questions.prompt: What do the tailors do when the bannock rolls in?
facilitatorNotes: They are dreadfully afraid and jump up to hide behind the goodwife. Ask why grown men would fear a little oatcake; the story is teasing them.
evidence: jumped up to hide behind the goodwife

questions.prompt: What do the tailors and the goodwife throw at the bannock? Does anything work?
facilitatorNotes: The iron, the ironing-board and the carders, and nothing hits it; it dodges out of the door.
evidence: Then the tailor cast the goose at it,
but it dodged them and trundled away gaily

questions.prompt: Why does the weaver want the bannock so much, and how does it get away?
facilitatorNotes: His porridge was thin this morning, so he is hungry. While his wife reaches and he shouts, the bannock dodges and races off over the hill “like a mad cow.”
evidence: for the porridge was thin the morn;
trundling away over the hill like a new tarred sheep or a mad cow!

readings.title: The Wee Bannock, part 3: the churn, the miller and the smith
readings.challenge: Notice what the people say and what they really mean.
readings.focus: The miller and the smith offer the bannock a bed, but the bannock guesses where that bed would be.
readings.context: Recap: the runaway oatcake has dodged an old wife, three frightened tailors and a weaver’s wife. A cowherd looks after cows; a churn is a tub for turning cream into butter. A miller grinds grain into meal, a kind of flour; a smithy is a blacksmith’s workshop; ale is a kind of beer. “Come in by” means come inside; quarters and lodging are places to stay.

excerpt.locator: “The Wee Bannock,” from the cowherd’s house to the smithy; opens “And it trundled away till it came to a cowherd's house where the goodwife was churning…”; closes “…out flax and combing it. So it ran into the fireside and began to toast itself again.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to the cowherd’s wife and her churn?
facilitatorNotes: Trying to grab the bannock, she knocks the churn over, and while she sets it straight the bannock rolls away.
evidence: the goodwife overset the churn in trying to grip it,

questions.prompt: The miller and the smith both tap their fat stomachs. What kind of “lodging” do they mean?
facilitatorNotes: Inside their stomachs: they mean to eat the bannock, with cheese or with ale. The stomach-tapping gives the joke away.
evidence: I'll give ye a night's quarters.
I'll give you a lodging inside.

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t the bannock trust them, and how does it escape the smith?
facilitatorNotes: It guesses they want to eat it, so it runs. The smith chases it and throws his hammer, but misses.
evidence: it wasn't going to trust itself with the miller and his cheese;
But the hammer missed

readings.title: The Wee Bannock, part 4: halves, soup and a shut door
readings.challenge: Watch plans go wrong, and judge which plan was the cleverest.
readings.focus: Three more households try sharing, throwing and shutting the door, and the bannock beats them all.
readings.context: Recap: the wee bannock has escaped a churning goodwife, a miller and a blacksmith, who all meant to eat it. Flax is a plant whose fibres are combed to make linen. “My certy” means “my word”; spirity means lively; tother means the other; afore means before. A thorn collar stops a calf from sucking.
readings.contentNote: A man falls among thorns and is scalded by hot soup.

excerpt.locator: “The Wee Bannock,” from the flax-combers’ farm to the house at supper; opens “"Janet," says the goodman, "yon is a well-toasted wee bannock. I'll have the half of it."”; closes “…his best hat, the wee bannock was too clever for them, and was out of sight in a crack.”.

questions.prompt: How do the farmer and his wife plan to share the bannock?
facilitatorNotes: Half each. But the bannock dodges, and the flax comb she throws misses.
evidence: I'll have the half of it.
And I'll take the tother half,

questions.prompt: What goes wrong in the house where the soup is cooking?
facilitatorNotes: The chair tips over, the goodman falls among the thorns, and the hot soup from the spoon spills on him; the bannock runs out.
evidence: down came the goodman among the thorns.
the scalding soup fell on the goodman and scalded him,

questions.prompt: At supper, the cautious goodman wants to shut the door first. Is that a good plan? Why does it fail?
facilitatorNotes: It is the cleverest plan so far, but he says it aloud: the bannock hears him and is off before the door is shut. Children may say he should have shut it quietly.
evidence: "Let's shut the door first," says the cautious goodman,
it judged it was time to be off;

readings.title: The Wee Bannock, part 5: the breeches and the fox
readings.challenge: Hear how the chase ends, and why the last host succeeds.
readings.focus: After escaping everyone, the bannock rolls into a fox’s hole, and the fox’s welcome is a trick.
readings.context: Recap: the wee bannock has rolled from house to house, and everyone who tried to catch it, with spoons, hats, soup and plans, has missed. Breeches are trousers that come to the knee; nigh means nearly; whins are prickly bushes, and a whinbush is one of them. Read the fox’s words in a friendly voice.

excerpt.locator: “The Wee Bannock,” from the house at bedtime to the end of the tale; opens “Then away it trundled till it came to a house where the folk were just away to their…”; closes “…two! For he snapped the wee bannock into halves with one bite. So that was an end of it!”.

questions.prompt: What does the goodman throw at the bannock, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: His breeches. The bannock wriggles out, and he chases it without them over the park and through the bushes, then comes back scratched and shivering.
evidence: So the goodman cast his breeches at it
the goodman after it without his breeches.

questions.prompt: Where does the bannock go when it is too dark to see?
facilitatorNotes: Into a fox’s hole in a big whinbush, to spend the night.
evidence: Then it came to a fox's hole in the side of a big whinbush

questions.prompt: The fox says, “I wish there were two of you!” What does he mean, and how does the story end?
facilitatorNotes: He has had no food for three days and wishes there were more to eat. He bites the bannock in half, so “there were two!” Children may feel sorry for the bannock, or say it should not have trusted a friendly welcome after running from everyone else.
evidence: You're welcome, friend! I wish there were two of you!
For he snapped the wee bannock into halves with one bite.

readings.title: How Jack Went Out to Seek His Fortune, part 1: the more the merrier
readings.workTitle: How Jack Went Out to Seek His Fortune
readings.challenge: Keep a growing list of travellers in order, then hear what their noise can do.
readings.focus: Jack welcomes every animal he meets, and together their noises frighten off a band of robbers.
readings.context: To seek your fortune is to go out into the world to find a good life. “The more the merrier” means more friends make more fun. “Jiggelty-jolt” is the bumpy sound of travelling. Robbers are thieves; a hubbub is a great noise. Let the child say “jiggelty-jolt” and make each animal’s sound. The tale ends tomorrow.

excerpt.locator: “How Jack Went Out to Seek His Fortune,” from the beginning to the robbers running away; opens “Once on a time there was a boy named Jack, and one morning he started to go and seek his…”; closes “…laugh, Jack and his companions went in and took possession of the house and the gold.”.

questions.prompt: Which animals join Jack, in order?
facilitatorNotes: A cat, a dog, a goat, a bull and a rooster. The child can count them on their fingers.
evidence: So on they went, Jack, the cat, the dog, the goat, the bull, and the rooster.

questions.prompt: What does Jack see through the window?
facilitatorNotes: A band of robbers at a table counting great bags of gold.
evidence: a band of robbers seated at a table counting over great bags of gold!

questions.prompt: How do Jack and the animals get the robbers out of the house? Why does it work?
facilitatorNotes: At Jack’s word they all make as much noise as they can, each in its own way, and the robbers run off in fright, perhaps thinking something huge is coming. Make the noises together.
evidence: make all the noise they possibly could in their own fashion.
the robbers jumped up in a fright and ran away,

readings.title: How Jack Went Out to Seek His Fortune, part 2: the robber’s fearsome tale
readings.workTitle: How Jack Went Out to Seek His Fortune
readings.challenge: Match each thing the frightened robber describes with the animal it really was.
readings.focus: In the dark, a robber mistakes the animals for fierce people, and Jack goes home with the gold.
readings.context: Recap: Jack set out with a cat, a dog, a goat, a bull and a rooster, and their noise frightened a band of robbers away from their gold. An awl is a sharp tool a shoemaker uses; threshing is beating grain out of straw with a flail, a stick with a swinging end. A guinea is a gold coin; booty is treasure. Read the robber’s tale in a scared voice and the “That was the cat, you know” lines quietly.
readings.contentNote: The animals scratch, bite, butt and knock down the robber, who thinks people attacked him with needles, an awl, a flail and an axe.

excerpt.locator: “How Jack Went Out to Seek His Fortune,” from bedtime in the robbers’ house to the end of the tale; opens “Now Jack was a wise boy, and he knew that the robbers would come back in the dead of the…”; closes “" Cock-a-doodle-do, Cook him in a stew!"”.

questions.prompt: Where does Jack put each animal before he goes to bed?
facilitatorNotes: The cat in the rocking-chair, the dog under the table, the goat upstairs, the bull in the cellar, and the rooster on the roof.
evidence: he put the cat in the rocking-chair,
and bade the rooster fly up on to the roof.

questions.prompt: The robber says an old woman stuck knitting-needles into him. Who was it really?
facilitatorNotes: The cat, scratching him with her claws. The child can match the others too: the shoemaker was the dog, the thresher the goat, the woodchopper the bull.
evidence: there was an old woman knitting there,
(That was the cat, you know.)

questions.prompt: What does the robber think the rooster was shouting? Why does Jack give the rooster a coin to carry in its beak?
facilitatorNotes: “Cook him in a stew!” when the rooster was only crowing “cock-a-doodle-do.” Jack gives it a gold coin to hold so that it cannot crow all the way home. Children may enjoy saying the two sounds one after the other.
evidence: 'Cook him in a stew! Cook him in a stew! Cook him in a stew!'
to prevent it from calling all the time:

readings.title: The Wise Men of Gotham: Of Buying of Sheep
readings.challenge: Work out what the two men are arguing about, and whether it is there at all.
readings.focus: Two men fight over sheep that do not exist, and a third man shows them how foolish that is.
readings.context: Gotham is a real village in England, and for hundreds of years people have told jokes about its foolish “wise men.” “Marry” was an old exclamation, like “Why!”; staves are walking sticks; strife is quarrelling; meal is ground grain, like flour; wit means good sense. The last sentence asks the listener to judge.

excerpt.locator: “The Wise Men of Gotham,” the episode “Of Buying of Sheep,” complete; opens “There were two men of Gotham, and one of them was going to market to Nottingham to buy…”; closes “Which was the wisest of these three persons, judge yourself.”.

questions.prompt: Where do the two men meet, and what do they quarrel about?
facilitatorNotes: On Nottingham bridge, about whether the sheep one of them means to buy may cross it.
evidence: they both met together upon Nottingham bridge
"Buy sheep?" said the other, "and which way will you bring them home?"

questions.prompt: How many sheep are really on the bridge?
facilitatorNotes: None. The men beat their sticks as if a hundred sheep were there; ask the child to listen for the words that show it.
evidence: as if there had been a hundred sheep between them

questions.prompt: Why does the third man shake his meal into the river? Was he the wisest of the three?
facilitatorNotes: To show that their heads hold as little sense as his empty sack holds meal. The story asks us to judge: he threw away his own meal to make his point, so a child who calls him foolish too has a fair reason.
evidence: how much meal is there in my sack?
Which was the wisest of these three persons, judge yourself.

readings.title: The Wise Men of Gotham: Of Hedging a Cuckoo
readings.challenge: Find the men’s plan and the reason it could never work.
readings.focus: The men try to keep spring all year by fencing in a bird that can fly.
readings.context: The cuckoo’s call is heard only in spring and early summer; then the bird flies away to warmer lands. A hedge is a wall of bushes; “round in compass” means in a circle. “A vengeance on her!” is an old curse, like “Bother her!”

excerpt.locator: “The Wise Men of Gotham,” the episode “Of Hedging a Cuckoo,” complete; opens “Once upon a time the men of Gotham would have kept the Cuckoo so that she might sing all…”; closes “…flew away. "A vengeance on her!" said they. "We did not make our hedge high enough."”.

questions.prompt: Why do the men of Gotham want to keep the cuckoo?
facilitatorNotes: So that she will sing all through the year, and spring will seem to last.
evidence: so that she might sing all the year

questions.prompt: What do they build to keep her in?
facilitatorNotes: A round hedge in the middle of their town.
evidence: in the midst of their town they made a hedge round in compass

questions.prompt: The men say their hedge was not high enough. What was their real mistake?
facilitatorNotes: A bird can fly over any hedge, and the cuckoo leaves with the season anyway. Some children will say a roof was needed; ask whether even a cage could keep the spring.
evidence: flew away
We did not make our hedge high enough.

readings.title: The Wise Men of Gotham: Of Drowning Eels
readings.challenge: Spot the two mistakes the villagers make.
readings.focus: The men of Gotham throw salted fish in a pond to breed, then punish an eel by putting it in water.
readings.context: Gotham is a real village in England, and for hundreds of years people have told jokes about its foolish “wise men.” Good Friday is the Friday before Easter. Herrings and sprats are small sea fish; salt fish has been dried and salted to keep, so it is no longer alive. To “fare like lords” is to eat like rich men; “shift for yourself” means look after yourself.
readings.contentNote: The men want to kill the eel, and decide to drown it.

excerpt.locator: “The Wise Men of Gotham,” the episode “Of Drowning Eels,” complete; opens “When Good Friday came, the men of Gotham cast their heads together what to do with their…”; closes “…shift for yourself, for no help thou shalt have from us"; and they left the eel to drown.”.

questions.prompt: What do the men put into their pond, and what do they hope will happen?
facilitatorNotes: Their salted fish, hoping it will breed so they can eat like lords next year. Ask whether dead, salted fish can have babies.
evidence: that they might breed against the next year,
we shall fare like lords next year.

questions.prompt: What do they find in the pond the next year, and who do they blame?
facilitatorNotes: Only a great eel, and they blame it for eating all their fish.
evidence: there was nothing but a great eel.
he has eaten up all our fish.

questions.prompt: How do they punish the eel? Why is that silly?
facilitatorNotes: They put it in another pond to drown. An eel is a fish and lives in water, so they have really set it free. Children who see the joke can explain it in their own words.
evidence: "Not so," said another; "let us drown him."
and they left the eel to drown.

readings.title: The Wise Men of Gotham: Of Sending Rent
readings.challenge: Guess what really happens to the money, though the story never says.
readings.focus: The men of Gotham trust a hare to deliver their rent, and explain away every sign that it is running off.
readings.context: Rent is money paid to a landlord for the use of land or a house. A purse is a small money bag. Lancaster, Loughborough and Newark are towns in England. “Light of foot” means a fast runner; subtle means clever; the highway is the main road.

excerpt.locator: “The Wise Men of Gotham,” the episode “Of Sending Rent,” complete; opens “Once on a time the men of Gotham had forgotten to pay their landlord. One said to the…”; closes “…"It is a subtle hare, let her alone; she will not keep the highway for fear of dogs."”.

questions.prompt: What have the men of Gotham forgotten to do?
facilitatorNotes: Pay their landlord his rent, and pay-day is tomorrow.
evidence: the men of Gotham had forgotten to pay their landlord.

questions.prompt: Who do they choose to carry the money, and why?
facilitatorNotes: A hare one of them has caught, because it is a fast runner. They tie the purse and letter round its neck.
evidence: This day I have caught a hare, and he shall carry it, for he is light of foot.

questions.prompt: When the hare runs off another way, what do the men say? Will the landlord get his money?
facilitatorNotes: They say it knows a nearer way, and that it keeps off the highway for fear of dogs. Almost certainly the hare has run home to the fields with the money. Children may also notice the men cannot decide whether the hare is “he” or “she.”
evidence: he can tell a nearer way than the best of us all.
she will not keep the highway for fear of dogs.

readings.title: The Wise Men of Gotham: Of Counting
readings.challenge: Find the counting mistake that every man makes.
readings.focus: Each man forgets to count himself, so they all mourn a neighbour who was never lost.
readings.context: Twelve men of Gotham go fishing. Ventured means taken risks; lamentation is loud crying; a courtier is a gentleman from a king’s court. Act out the counting with twelve toys, leaving out the one that does the counting.
readings.contentNote: The courtier hits each man to “count” him and takes all their money, and the men thank him.

excerpt.locator: “The Wise Men of Gotham,” the episode “Of Counting,” complete; opens “On a certain time there were twelve men of Gotham who went fishing, and some went into…”; closes “"God bless you on your heart," said all the company; "you have found our neighbour."”.

questions.prompt: How many men went fishing, and how many does each man count?
facilitatorNotes: Twelve went fishing, but each man counts eleven.
evidence: Twelve of us came out.
every man did count eleven

questions.prompt: Why does each man count only eleven?
facilitatorNotes: He never counts himself. Try it with toys, then ask the child who was left out.
evidence: the twelfth man did never count himself

questions.prompt: How does the courtier find the twelfth man? Was he being kind?
facilitatorNotes: He whacks each man as he counts, ending with “Here is the twelfth man.” He solves the puzzle, but he hurts them and takes all their money, and they thank him anyway. Children may call him clever or a bully; both can use the story.
evidence: Give me the money,
Here is the twelfth man.
